extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, poets, and students of dramatic theory (writers of tragedy)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating tragic plays: how to construct plots, incidents of recognition and reversal, arrange the quantitative parts of a tragedy, and portray character so as to produce pity and fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot parts: Reversal, Recognition, Tragic Incident
rubrics_metrics.description: Two parts of the plot—Reversal of Intention and Recognition—turn upon surprises. A third part is the Tragic Incident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognition is between persons and may be one-sided or mutual (examples: Iphigenia revealed to Orestes by a letter but Orestes must be recognised by Iphigenia by another act). The Tragic Incident is a destructive or painful action (such as death, agony, wounds and the like).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative parts of tragedy (dramatic divisions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is divided quantitatively into Prologue, Episode, Exodos, and Choric song (the Choric song being divided into Parodos and Stasimon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Prologos precedes the Parodos. The Episode is that part between complete choric songs. The Exodos is that part with no choric song after it. The Parodos is the Chorus' first undivided utterance; the Stasimon is a choric ode without anapaests or trochaic tetrameters. The Commos is a joint lamentation of Chorus and actors. Some plays also have songs of actors from the stage and the Commos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrange plots on the complex (not simple) plan to excite pity and fear
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should arrange the plot on the complex plan; it should imitate actions which excite pity and fear—the distinctive mark of tragic imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The change of fortune must be such as to arouse pity and fear; the poet should aim at producing these emotions by the inner structure of the piece rather than by mere spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate form of change of fortune (who suffers and why)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid presenting (a) a virtuous man brought from prosperity to adversity, (b) a bad man passing from adversity to prosperity, or (c) the downfall of an utter villain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The best tragic protagonist is a person between extremes—illustrious and prosperous yet with some great error or frailty (not vice) that brings about the reversal. Such a fall excites pity (unmerited misfortune) and fear (misfortune of a man like ourselves).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity / singleness of issue
rubrics_metrics.description: A well-constructed plot should be single in its issue rather than double.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best tragedies are founded on the story of a few houses (a few families) and a single resulting catastrophe; double-thread plots may please weak spectators and resemble epic forms (e.g., the Odyssey) but do not produce the true tragic pleasure as effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inner structure preferred to spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: Pity and fear may be aroused by spectacle, but they are better produced by the inner structure of the piece.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producing tragic effect by spectacle (making the monstrous visible) is a less artistic method and dependent on extraneous aids; superior poets create the effect such that 'he who hears the tale' will thrill without needing visual spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of tragic incidents by relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions capable of exciting pity or terror should occur between persons who are friends, enemies, or indifferent; they are most effective when among those who are near or dear to one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Situations like a brother killing a brother, a son his father, a mother her son, etc., are particularly suitable. Poets should not destroy received legends but should invent and skilfully handle traditional material to produce the tragic quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds and ranking of how a dreadful deed may occur
rubrics_metrics.description: The deed may be: (1) done consciously with knowledge of the persons; (2) done in ignorance with the tie discovered afterwards; (3) one is about to act with knowledge and then refrains (worst); (4) one is about to act in ignorance and discovers before doing it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Of these, the best is that the deed is perpetrated in ignorance and the discovery is made afterwards (startling and tragic). The worst is being about to act knowing the persons and then not acting—shocking without tragic consequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character: goodness (primary requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Character in tragedy must be good (first and most important). Any speech or action that manifests moral purpose will be perceived as character: the character will be good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goodness is relative to class—women and slaves may be good within their class. Goodness is essential because tragedy arouses moral reactions (pity and fear).

rubrics_metrics.name: Character: propriety / fitness
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters must display propriety—qualities appropriate to their class and role (e.g., manly courage is sometimes found in a woman but is not generally appropriate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is a type of manly valour; this quality is not generally appropriate to women. The poet should aim at types that are proper to the character's class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character: consistency (and consistent inconsistency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters must be consistent: even if 'inconsistent' in their moral condition, they must be consistently so (the subject of imitation must act by necessity or probability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid motiveless degradation, indecorous or inappropriate speeches/actions, and sudden unmotivated changes (e.g., Iphigenia at Aulis inconsistent with her later self). Character actions should follow necessity or probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actions and unraveling must arise from the plot (avoid Deus ex Machina)
rubrics_metrics.description: Complication and unravelling of the plot must arise out of the plot itself; the Deus ex Machina must not be used for events internal to the drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deus ex Machina may be employed only for events external to the drama (antecedent or subsequent events beyond human knowledge). Using it to resolve internal problems is an artistic fault (examples: Medea, Return of the Greeks in the Iliad).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition: kinds and artistic merit
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognitions may occur by signs (congenital or acquired), tokens/formal proof, a turn of incident, poet-invented speech, objects evoking memory, or process of reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tokens and formal proofs are less artistic. A turn of incident (e.g., Bath Scene in the Odyssey) is better. Poet-invented recognitions (where the poet makes a character announce himself without plot necessity) are lacking in art. The best recognitions are those arising naturally from incidents or from plausible reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition by signs and tokens (specifics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Signs: congenital (e.g., spear-mark), acquired (scars), external tokens (necklaces, little ark). Tokens used solely for proof are less artistic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even tokens admit more or less skilful treatment (Odysseus' scar treated skilfully by different agents—nurse, herdsmen). The use of tokens for express proof lacks art compared to recognitions arising from incident or reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition by reasoning and by incident preferred
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognitions by process of reasoning or by a turn of incident are more artistic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: reasoning ('no one resembles me but Orestes, therefore Orestes has come'); a turn of incident (Bath Scene). These yield natural discoveries that avoid artificial token proofs or poet-invented announcements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid poet-invented recognitions (authorial contrivance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognitions invented at will by the poet (e.g., a character revealing himself by speech when the plot does not require it) are not artistic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such contrivances are allied to the fault of using external devices to force recognition and reduce the plausibility and causality of the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain rationality within the action
rubrics_metrics.description: Within the action there must be nothing irrational; if the irrational cannot be excluded, it should lie outside the scope of the tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rational coherence is part of the tragic effect (example: rational element in Sophocles' Oedipus). Irrational causes or resolutions inside the play damage artistic integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayal of character: ennoble the type
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should, like a good portrait-painter, reproduce the distinctive form of the original but make a likeness which is true to life and yet more beautiful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While preserving the type (irascible, indolent, etc.), the poet should ennoble the character in representation (example: Achilles in Agathon and Homer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Stagecraft: place the scene vividly and use appropriate gestures
rubrics_metrics.description: In constructing and working out the plot and diction the poet should place the scene, as far as possible, before his eyes and work with appropriate gestures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seeing everything vividly helps discover what is in keeping with the action and avoid inconsistencies. Actors should show natural emotion (those who feel emotion are convincing through natural sympathy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition method: outline first, then episodes and detail
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should first sketch the general outline of the story and then fill in the episodes and amplify in detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Iphigenia: sketch the young girl's fate and broad movements, then fill in specific incidents, modes of recognition, and how the action brings about the final consequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of sensory and dictional appeals as concomitants
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeals to the senses and appropriate diction are not essentials but are concomitants of poetry, and there is much room for error in them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poet should attend to diction and sensory appeals but prioritize structure and character; for these matters further guidance is in other treatises (per author).
